children: Hungary's central bank needs to maintain a sufficient buffer in terms of real interest rates amid volatility in global markets driven by conflicts such as
central bank Governor Mihaly Varga told an economics conference on Thursday.

Last month the bank delivered its third successive quarter-point rate cut, as expected, to 5.5%, and left the door open to further rate easing depending on its September inflation projections and global market developments.

However, on Thursday Varga struck a cautious tone, saying despite steep falls in Hungary's inflation rate, which ran at 1.3% in August, a disciplined monetary policy framework was needed amid serious global inflation risks.

"We believe that we must provide sufficient protection against the current uncertainties in the global economy," Varga said, adding that the bank was prepared to gradually lower its 3% inflation target as part of Hungary's euro adoption efforts.
He said Hungary's real interest rate level could fall if the country makes progress towards adopting the euro. The central bank's next policy meeting is due on September 22.

Prime Minister Peter Magyar's pro-European Union turn since his April election victory has triggered a sharp rally in Hungarian assets, curbing bond yields and sending the forint to five-year highs against the euro.

The war in Iran and surging energy prices have pared some of those gains. Market volatility and risks from weak demographics and higher debt levels meant Hungary's path to joining the euro could be more challenging compared with some of its peers, Varga said.
"We have started off adopting the euro in a more difficult context for the world economy, where success is not so self-evident as it used to be," he said.
REVIVING GROWTH AND CURBING DEFICIT ARE KEY CHALLENGES

Varga said a key challenge would be to revive Hungary's economic growth and narrow the yawning budget deficit, which at 7.5% of economic output could be the EU's widest this year and more than twice the maximum 3% gap allowed for joining the euro.

Finance Minister Andras Karman said the government, which plans to present a medium-term fiscal path this year on how it aims to meet euro entry criteria by 2030, would focus on spending cuts rather than tax hikes to curb the shortfall.
He said this strategy could ensure that Hungary's growth, which has stalled in the past three years, would not be hit by the fiscal adjustment measures.

"Against all challenges, the inflowing EU funds, reviving external demand, and hopefully the central bank's reopening room for manoeuvre combined will replace the demand temporarily curbed by the (fiscal) tightening," he said.
